schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE PAYROLL (SSNO INT, DEPTNO INT);
CREATE TABLE APPLICANT (SSNO INT, JOBTITILE INT, OFFICENO INT);
q1: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL AS X, APPLICANT AS Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL AS A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL AS Y) AS B, APPLICANT AS C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT Y.* FROM PAYROLL AS X, APPLICANT AS Y WHERE X.SSNO = Y.SSNO AND X.DEPTNO = 29
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT C.* FROM PAYROLL AS A, (SELECT Y.SSNO, Y.DEPTNO FROM PAYROLL AS Y) AS B, APPLICANT AS C WHERE A.SSNO = B.SSNO AND C.SSNO = A.SSNO AND B.DEPTNO = 29
counterexample: INSERT INTO PAYROLL (SSNO, DEPTNO) VALUES (1, 29), (1, 30), (2, 29); INSERT INTO APPLICANT (SSNO, JOBTITILE, OFFICENO) VALUES (1, 1, 101), (2, 2, 102);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent because Q1 directly selects all columns from the APPLICANT table where the SSNO matches in the PAYROLL table and the DEPTNO is 29. Q2, on the other hand, first selects the SSNO and DEPTNO from the PAYROLL table, then uses these results to join with the APPLICANT table, which can lead to different results if there are multiple records in the PAYROLL table for the same SSNO.
counterexample_dsp: In Q1, if an applicant has multiple payroll records in department 29, all of them will be selected. In Q2, only the first record of the subquery for each applicant will be used, potentially missing other payroll records in department 29.
